plan.contextChunk: This figure contains four sub-panels (a through d) showing the different matrix representations used to encode a graph for graph neural networks. Panel a) depicts a 6-node undirected graph with nodes labeled 1 through 6, connected by edges whose identities are marked by the pair of endpoint node labels (e.g., ‘1\3’, ‘1\4’, ‘2\3’, ‘3\4’, ‘3\6’, ‘4\5’, ‘5\6’). Panel b) shows the adjacency matrix A (N × N), a square binary matrix encoding which pairs of nodes are connected by edges. Panel c) shows the node feature matrix X (D × N), in which each column stores the D-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the N nodes. Panel d) shows the edge feature matrix E (Dᴷ × E), in which each column stores the Dᴷ-dimensional feature vector associated with one of the E edges, with edges ordered to match the labeled pairs in panel a). Labels for each matrix include its name, symbol, and dimensions. This figure introduces the three standard data structures—adjacency matrix, node feature matrix, and edge feature matrix—that together fully represent a graph with node and edge attributes in a deep learning context.

interactionPlan.concept: A graph with node and edge attributes is fully encoded by three matrices — the adjacency matrix A (connectivity), the node data matrix X (one feature column per node), and the edge data matrix E (one feature column per edge) — and every element of the visual graph maps to a specific location in each matrix.
elements: panel labels 'a)', 'b)', 'c)', 'd)'
panel a: six node circles labeled 1–6 with dark brown outlines, arranged with node 2 upper-left, node 1 upper-center, node 4 upper-right-of-center, node 3 mid-left, node 5 right, node 6 bottom-center
panel a: seven undirected teal edges: 1–3, 1–4, 2–3, 3–4, 3–6, 4–5, 5–6
panel a: beside each node, a short vertical stack of small squares in brown/orange shades (that node's feature vector)
panel a: beside each edge, a short vertical stack of small squares in teal/green shades (that edge's feature vector)
panel b: title 'Adjacency matrix, A' with subtitle 'N × N' in dark slate blue

panel b: 6×6 grid with row labels 1–6 (left) and column labels 1–6 (top); dark slate filled cells at (1,3),(1,4),(2,3),(3,1),(3,2),(3,4),(3,6),(4,1),(4,3),(4,5),(5,4),(5,6),(6,3),(6,5) — symmetric with empty diagonal
panel c: title 'Node data, X' with subtitle 'D × N' in brown
panel c: grid of 4 rows × 6 columns, column headers 1–6, cells in varied brown/orange shades matching each node's feature stack
panel d: title 'Edge data, E' with subtitle 'D_E × E' in teal

panel d: grid of 4 rows × 7 columns with two header rows giving edge endpoint pairs '1\3', '1\4', '2\3', '3\4', '3\6', '4\5', '5\6', cells in varied teal/green shades matching each edge's feature stack

interactions.teaches: A node is not just a circle — it owns a row AND a column of the adjacency matrix A (its filled cells list exactly its neighbors) and one column of the node data matrix X (its feature vector, the same stack of squares drawn beside it in the graph)

An edge corresponds to two symmetric filled cells in A (one at (i,j) and one at (j,i), because the graph is undirected), to one labeled column of the edge data matrix E holding its feature vector, and to the two endpoint nodes it connects

interactions.label: Focus representation
interactions.teaches: The four panels are not four different datasets but four views of one object — isolating each shows what that representation alone captures (structure in A, node attributes in X, edge attributes in E) and what it leaves out

demo_steps.title: One graph, four views
demo_steps.narration: Panel a shows the graph as a picture: six nodes, seven edges, and a small colored feature stack attached to every node (brown) and every edge (teal). Panels b, c, and d store exactly the same information as matrices that a neural network can consume.

demo_steps.title: Click node 3
demo_steps.narration: Click node 3 — the best-connected node. Its row and column light up in A (four filled cells = four neighbors: 1, 2, 4, 6), and column 3 of X lights up, matching the brown feature stack drawn beside it in the graph.

demo_steps.title: Click edge 3–4
demo_steps.narration: Now click the edge between nodes 3 and 4. Two symmetric cells of A highlight — (3,4) and (4,3) — because an undirected edge is recorded twice, and the column of E labeled '3\4' highlights, holding this edge's teal feature vector.

demo_steps.title: Isolate each matrix
demo_steps.narration: Use the focus toggle to view A, X, and E one at a time: A alone knows only who is connected, X alone knows only node attributes, E alone knows only edge attributes — only together do they reconstruct panel a.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Everything in the graph picture has an exact address in the matrices: a node is a row-plus-column of A and a column of X, and an edge is a symmetric pair of cells in A and a column of E — so A, X, and E together are a complete, machine-readable encoding of the graph.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Four-panel layout matching the source: panel a (graph) large on the left, panel b (adjacency matrix) top-center, panel c (node data) top-right, panel d (edge data) bottom-center-right. Graph nodes are white circles with dark brown outlines and black numeral labels; edges are muted dark teal lines. Node feature stacks use a warm brown/orange/tan palette; edge feature stacks use a teal/mint palette — this brown=nodes, teal=edges color coding is carried into panels c and d and is essential to the cross-panel correspondence. In panel b, filled cells are dark slate blue on a white grid with gray cell borders, empty diagonal, and the pattern must be symmetric. Panels c and d cells are colored squares with varied shades (c: browns; d: teals) with white grid gaps; panel d has two stacked header rows so each column reads as an endpoint pair like '1\3'. Matrix titles are italic serif: name and symbol (e.g. 'Adjacency matrix, A') above dimension ('N × N'), colored to match their content (slate for A, brown for X, teal for E). Highlighting on selection should use a bright accent outline/glow on the node circle or edge line plus the corresponding matrix row/column/cells, so the graph-to-matrix mapping is unmistakable.
